evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 形義源流通解; 甲骨文 and 金文 usage
evidence.text: The database describes 人 in ancient forms as a person standing in profile with hands lowered; it gives the original sense as ‘person’. It cites Shang oracle-bone examples 《合集》22626 ‘伐十人’ (ten people killed) and 《合集》20328 ‘余一人’ (the king’s self-reference), and bronze-inscription uses including ‘庶人’ (common people) and ‘人民’. It also reports a bronze-inscription phonetic loan 人 for 年 in one vessel inscription, a separate graph borrowing from 人’s role as sound element in 年.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析: 人

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry identifies the graph in oracle-bone inscriptions (合集6175), bronze inscriptions (集成00944), and the Small Seal script / Shuowen. Its account interprets the profile figure’s upper end as the head, middle as body, one extended stroke as arm, and lower part as legs. This supports a human-figure pictograph analysis; the stroke-by-stroke description is the database’s interpretation, not a separately demonstrated chronology.

evidence.text: The entry quotes Shuowen’s account that 人 depicts arm and shin forms, then cautions that certain ‘ancient’ shapes reported in later reference works are not found in oracle-bone, bronze, or ancient Zhou-script materials and their evidence is unknown. gaps: The oldest forms are labelled oracle-bone and bronze forms in the paleographic database, but the inspected page does not date the individual cited specimens; the oracle-bone corpus context is broadly Late Shang, not a character-specific first-use date.
No independent external verification of the supplied Baxter–Sagart table row was possible, and no same-system comparison is needed for 人 itself because it has no proposed sound component.

The official character-specific Unihan endpoint https://www.unicode.org/cgi-bin/GetUnihanData.pl?codepoint=4EBA was attempted but inaccessible in the web tool. The local exact kMandarin row was supplied and retained as local metadata only; it is not represented as externally verified.

Shuowen’s account is an early historical explanation, not independent confirmation of a pristine pictorial origin. Inspected modern paleographic references support the side-profile human interpretation, but no glyph image was visually inspected in this research.

The source database offers selected older semantic uses, but not a systematic chronology of all extensions such as individual, people, someone, or other person. No chronology is inferred from modern gloss lists.

The reported 人-for-夷 and 人-for-年 loans are source assertions. Their precise early pronunciations and the phonological basis of each loan were not independently established in this search. No claim is made that 人 derives from 仁 or vice versa.
No individual date was found for cited oracle-bone specimen references; the sources classify them as oracle-bone material but do not supply a character-specific first-use date.

The sources identify the original sense as ‘person’ and provide Shang oracle-bone instances, then list later bronze and textual uses such as common people, people/population, and ruler’s self-reference. They do not provide a complete dated semantic chronology or prove every link between these uses.

The reported whole-graph loans 人-for-夷 and 人-for-年 are not independently phonologically established in the inspected evidence. The separate statement that 人 functions as 年’s phonetic element does not itself establish the sound basis for the whole-graph loan.

Shuowen’s explanation is preserved as a historical account, not independent proof. The inspected paleographic descriptions support a human profile interpretation; the Taiwan MOE entry warns that some forms later labelled ancient lack attestation in early corpora.

The character-specific Unicode Unihan endpoint failed to load. The local kMandarin and Baxter–Sagart rows remain local metadata; current reading metadata is not evidence of ancient sound relationships.
The selected historical glyphs are modern vector redrawings. The web tool could not fetch their SVG pixels, so no visual inspection is claimed.
